pos: n. (Jacobus Alting, 1618–1679, Hebraist and professor of Oriental languages and theology at Groningen)
etymology: Alting, a Frisian and Westphalian family name; Jacobus, the Latin form of Hebrew Ya'aqob, Jacob, a heel-catcher, a supplanter.
biblical_def: Jacobus Alting was the son of Heinrich Alting and the grandson of Menso Alting, the third of a line of Reformed divines running from Emden to Heidelberg to Groningen. Born at Heidelberg, he studied there and at Groningen, learned Hebrew in London from the Jewish teacher Jacob Abendana, was ordained in England, and in 1643 was made professor of Hebrew and the Oriental tongues at Groningen, adding the chair of theology in 1667. His whole labour was to read the Old Testament in its own language and grammar. He wrote a Hebrew grammar, a Hebrew-point treatise, a Syriac and a Chaldee grammar, and commentaries which took the plain grammatical sense of the words first and the rabbinical tradition afterward, and only as a witness. That method set him against his Groningen colleague Samuel Maresius, who charged him with Judaizing, with slighting the received Hebrew vowel system, and with Coccejan novelty in the covenants. The quarrel ran for sixteen years, cost both men peace, and was never properly settled; the States of the province at last forbade them to write against each other. Alting's works were gathered after his death in five folio volumes. He stands in the dictionary as a reminder that a Reformed man's first duty to the Old Testament is to construe it, and that a doctrine of Scripture which does not issue in grammar is not yet a doctrine of Scripture.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a professor as one who publicly teaches a science in a college; grammar as the art of speaking or writing a language with propriety; and to study as to apply the mind to books and learning.
webster_full: PROFESSOR, n. One who publicly teaches any science or branch of learning; particularly, an officer in a university or college, whose business is to read lectures or instruct students in a particular branch.
GRAMMAR, n. [L. grammatica.] The art of speaking or writing a language with propriety or correctness, according to established usage.
STUDY, v.i. To fix the mind closely upon a subject; to muse; to dwell upon in thought; to apply the mind to books.
TONGUE, n. The instrument of taste and of speech; hence, a language; the whole sum of words used by a particular nation.
CONTEND, v.i. To strive in opposition; to struggle in argument; to dispute earnestly.
scriptures: Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
Pro 4:7
Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding.
corruption_summary: Groningen Hebraist whose grammatical reading of the Old Testament against the rabbinical tradition drew a sixteen-year charge of Judaizing from his own colleague.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is nearer home. Alting's method—construe the Hebrew first, weigh the tradition after—is the method the historical-critical school later claimed as its own invention, and it was neither invented by that school nor owned by it. The difference is not grammar but authority. Alting took the text as the word of God and used grammar to hear it; the later school took grammar as a tool for deciding which parts of the text were the word of God and which were a later hand's. The dictionary keeps the grammar and refuses the authority claim.

The principle to recover is that learning in a minister is not a decoration. “rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15) is a workman's phrase, and the workman needs tools. Alting's quarrel with Maresius was a real fault on both sides—two orthodox men who could not distinguish a difference of method from a difference of faith, and who spent sixteen years proving it. The province was right to silence them both.

“So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly” (Neh 8:8) — the grammatical sense taken first, the rabbinical tradition weighed after.
“searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11) — five folio volumes gathered after his death in 1679.

pos: n. (Regnerus Praedinius, c. 1510–1559, rector of the school of St Martin at Groningen)
etymology: Praedinius, a Latinised form from the Frisian hamlet of Praedinge or Winsum; Regnerus, Latinised from the Frisian Reiner, from Germanic ragin, counsel, and heri, host.
biblical_def: Regnerus Praedinius was born in the Frisian countryside near Winsum and became, in 1541, rector of the great school of St Martin at Groningen, which under him drew scholars from the whole north. He was a schoolmaster rather than a controversialist, and his Reformation was the Reformation of the classroom: Greek and Hebrew taught to boys, the fathers read whole, Scripture construed in the original instead of recited in the Vulgate. In the line of Wessel Gansfort before him he held and taught that the bread and wine are not changed in substance, that the saints are not to be invoked, and that Scripture is the judge of the church's traditions—and he taught these things without ever leaving the old communion or signing a Protestant confession, which is why Rome suspected him and the Reformed could not quite claim him. He died in 1559, before Groningen was taken for the Republic and before the province had to choose. His pupils made the choice for him: from his benches came the men who carried the Reformation into Friesland and Groningen in the next generation, and the city's later university counted him among its fathers. He is entered here as the plainest instance of a truth the dictionary keeps repeating—that the Reformation travelled first along a schoolmaster's desk, and that the man who teaches a boy his Greek paradigms may be doing more for the gospel than the man who preaches to a thousand.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a rector as the chief elective officer of some universities; a school as a place of instruction in any species of learning; and to instruct as to teach, to inform the mind.
webster_full: RECTOR, n. [L. from rego, to rule.] A ruler; a governor; the chief elective officer of some universities; the head master of a school.
SCHOOL, n. [L. schola.] A place or house in which persons are instructed in arts, science, languages, or any species of learning.
INSTRUCT, v.t. [L. instruo.] To teach; to inform the mind; to communicate knowledge to; to educate.
LEARNING, n. The knowledge of principles or facts received by instruction or study; literature; erudition.
FORERUNNER, n. One who goes before another; a messenger sent before to prepare the way; a harbinger.
scriptures: Pro 9:9
Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser: teach a just man, and he will increase in learning.
And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
The words of the wise are as goads, and as nails fastened by the masters of assemblies, which are given from one shepherd.
Mal 2:7
For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth: for he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts.
corruption_summary: Groningen schoolmaster who taught the substance of the Reformation from the desk of St Martin's school without ever formally leaving the old communion.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The honest difficulty is Praedinius himself. A man who held the Reformed doctrine of the Supper, denied the invocation of saints, and set Scripture over tradition, and who yet never separated, is claimed too easily by both sides. Rome has made him a loyal Catholic humanist; some Reformed writers have made him a crypto-Protestant. The dictionary states its reading: he held several of the Reformation's doctrines truly and he did not take the Reformation's step, and the second fact is a real fault and not a nuance. A doctrine confessed only in a lecture hall has not yet been confessed.

The principle to recover is the dignity of the second rank. “the same commit thou to faithful men” (2Ti 2:2) is the whole of his service, and it was enough: the men who did take the step were his pupils. The church that despises its schoolmasters will have no preachers in twenty years.

“who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2) — his pupils carried the Reformation into Friesland and Groningen.
“as nails fastened by the masters of assemblies” (Ecc 12:11) — Greek and Hebrew taught to boys, the fathers read whole.

pos: n. (Johannes Acronius, 1565–1627, Frisian minister, professor at Franeker, and delegate to the Synod of Dort)
etymology: Acronius, a Latinised Frisian name taken from Akkrum in Friesland; Johannes, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious.
biblical_def: Johannes Acronius was a Frisian, trained at Franeker and Heidelberg, who served the churches at Wezep, Schoonhoven, Haarlem and Deventer before he was called in 1615 to the chair of theology at Franeker. He was known in his own province for two things. The first was disputation with the Mennonites, whom Friesland had in greater numbers than any other region of the Netherlands; he met them in public conference and in print, pressing the covenant promise to the children of believers and the lawfulness of the magistrate and of the oath. The second was the Arminian controversy, in which he stood with Bogerman, Lubbertus and Maccovius for the received doctrine, and in which he sat as one of the delegates of Friesland in the National Synod at Dordrecht in 1618 and 1619, subscribing the Canons and the sentence on the Remonstrants. He died at Franeker in 1627. His name is worth keeping because the Frisian delegation at Dort was not a bench of famous men: it was a bench of working pastors who had already argued the covenant with Anabaptists in their own market towns, and who came to Dordrecht knowing exactly what a doctrine costs when it is contradicted by a neighbour rather than by a book.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a synod as an ecclesiastical council; a delegate as a person appointed to act for another; and to dispute as to contend in argument.
webster_full: SYNOD, n. [Gr. a meeting.] A council or meeting of ecclesiastics to consult on matters of religion; an assembly of ministers and elders.
DELEGATE, n. [L. delego.] A person appointed and sent by another with powers to transact business as his representative.
DISPUTE, v.i. To contend in argument; to reason or argue in opposition; to debate; to altercate.
COVENANT, n. [L. convenio.] A mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons; in theology, a solemn compact between God and man.
SUBSCRIBE, v.t. To write under; to sign with one's own hand; to assent to by signing one's name.
scriptures: Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
Gen 17:7
And I will establish my covenant between me and thee and thy seed after thee in their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God unto thee, and to thy seed after thee.
Act 2:41
Then they that gladly received his word were baptized: and the same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls.
Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
corruption_summary: Franeker professor and Frisian delegate to Dort, who argued the covenant promise against the Mennonites of his own province before he argued election against the Remonstrants.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary must, however, state its own position where Acronius's is not its own. He pressed infant baptism from the covenant made with Abraham and his seed, and on that point the 1689 London Baptist Confession parts from him: the dictionary holds believer's baptism by immersion as the New Testament pattern, and reads the covenant promise as fulfilled in the gathering of a believing church rather than in the baptism of the children of the church. His argument against the Mennonites on the magistrate and the oath it holds with him entirely.

The principle to recover is that a doctrine is tested where it is contradicted. “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3) was for Acronius a thing done in a Frisian market town against his own neighbours before it was done in a national synod. Men who have never had to answer a serious objection in their own street should be slow to write about controversy.

“that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9) — delegate of Friesland at Dordrecht, 1618 and 1619.

pos: n. (Ubbo Emmius, 1547–1625, historian of Frisia and first rector of the university of Groningen)
etymology: Emmius, a Latinised Frisian patronymic from Emme; Ubbo, a Frisian given name, probably from Germanic wulf or ubbo, used of a chief.
biblical_def: Ubbo Emmius was born at Greetsiel in East Frisia, studied at Rostock and Geneva, and was a schoolmaster at Norden, Leer and Groningen for thirty years before the city made him, in 1614, the first rector of its new university. He was a convinced and unbending Calvinist. At Norden his insistence on the Reformed doctrine of the Supper against the Lutheran party cost him his post; at Groningen his insistence on the received doctrine against the Remonstrants kept the new university from the Arminian drift that unsettled Leiden. His great work was the history of Frisia, written in sixty books from the sources, in which he set out to do for his own province what the humanist historians had done for Italy, and to do it without the legends. He dated, compared and discarded; he refused the invented ancestries by which the Frisian nobility had traced itself to Troy; and he quarrelled publicly with those who preferred the legends because they were flattering. He died at Groningen in 1625, still rector. The dictionary keeps him for the discipline of his history. A man who will not flatter his own nation with a false pedigree has learned something that a man who handles Scripture needs: that a record is not improved by being embellished, and that the honour of a people is not served by lies told about its past.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines history as a narration of events in the order in which they happened; a legend as a chronicle or register of the lives of saints, formerly read at matins; and to record as to register, to preserve in writing.
webster_full: HISTORY, n. [L. historia.] An account of facts, particularly of facts respecting nations or states; a narration of events in the order of time in which they happened.
LEGEND, n. [L. legenda, to be read.] A chronicle or register of the lives of saints, formerly read at matins; hence, an idle or unfounded story.
RECORD, v.t. [L. recordor.] To register; to enroll; to write or enter in a book for the purpose of preserving authentic evidence of a fact.
RECTOR, n. The chief elective officer of some universities, as in France and Scotland; a governor.
PEDIGREE, n. Lineage; line of ancestors from which a person descends; genealogy.
scriptures: Hab 2:2
And the LORD answered me, and said, Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it.
Jer 36:4
Then Jeremiah called Baruch the son of Neriah: and Baruch wrote from the mouth of Jeremiah all the words of the LORD, which he had spoken unto him, upon a roll of a book.
Rom 15:4
For whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope.
Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth.
corruption_summary: Frisian historian and first rector of Groningen, who wrote his province's history from the sources and threw out the flattering legends.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the one Emmius fought: a nation's history written to flatter the nation. The Frisian gentry wanted a descent from Troy and resented the man who took it away. Every people has its version of this, and the Christian version is worse, because a church that invents a golden age for itself is lying about the work of God. The dictionary names the temptation plainly and refuses it in its own pages.

The principle to recover is that honesty about the past is a form of reverence. “Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables” (Hab 2:2) is a command to record, not to improve; and the written word of God is itself a record which does not spare its own heroes—Noah drunk, Abraham lying, David murdering, Peter denying. A history which would not have recorded those things is not fit to be read beside the Bible.

“written aforetime were written for our learning” (Rom 15:4) — first rector of the university of Groningen, 1614.
“Sanctify them through thy truth” (Joh 17:17) — the invented descent from Troy thrown out, and the nobility offended.

pos: n. (Tobias Andreae, 1604–1676, professor of Greek and history at Groningen, and a defender of the new philosophy)
etymology: Andreae, a Latinised patronymic from Andreas; Tobias, from Hebrew Tobiyah, the LORD is good.
biblical_def: Tobias Andreae was born at Braunfels in Nassau, studied at Herborn and Leiden, travelled as a tutor, and in 1635 was made professor of Greek and history at Groningen, where he taught for forty years. He is remembered for the part he took in the quarrel over Descartes. When the new philosophy was attacked in the Netherlands as a road to atheism, Andreae answered the attacks in three published defences, holding that a method of doubt applied to the natural world is not a doubt of God, and that the church does nothing for the faith by binding it to Aristotle. Against him stood men of his own confession who judged, not without reason, that a philosophy which begins from the thinking self will end by making the self the judge of revelation. The dictionary does not take the Cartesian side. It records instead what the quarrel shows: that orthodox and godly men in the same Reformed church could divide over the question of how far a Christian may use a philosophical method without adopting its first principle, and that neither party had the whole of the matter. Andreae was right that Aristotle is not an article of faith and that the schoolmen's physics is not the Bible's. His opponents were right that the Cartesian beginning, followed consistently, makes human reason the court of appeal; the next century proved them so. He died at Groningen in 1676.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines philosophy as the knowledge of the causes of all phenomena; doubt as a fluctuation of mind respecting truth; and reason as the faculty of comparing propositions and deducing consequences.
webster_full: PHILOSOPHY, n. [Gr. love of wisdom.] Literally, the love of wisdom; in modern acceptation, the knowledge of the phenomena of nature and of the reasons and causes of them.
DOUBT, n. A fluctuation of mind respecting truth or propriety, arising from defect of knowledge or evidence; uncertainty.
REASON, n. [L. ratio.] That intellectual faculty by which we compare propositions, deduce consequences, and distinguish truth from falsehood.
METHOD, n. [Gr. after, and a way.] A suitable and convenient arrangement of things, proceedings or ideas; orderly procedure.
CAPTIVITY, n. The state of being a prisoner; subjection; bondage; servitude.
scriptures: Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
Pro 4:7
Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding.
Then opened he their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures,
Joh 8:32
And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.
corruption_summary: Groningen professor of Greek who defended the Cartesian method against his own party, in a quarrel in which neither side had the whole of the matter.
corruption_paragraphs: The genuine corruption at stake is older than Descartes and outlived him: the making of human reason into the judge of revelation. Andreae did not intend it, and said so; but a method which begins by doubting everything until the thinking self certifies it does, when carried through, put the self in the chair. The eighteenth century carried it through, and the result was a theology which kept the vocabulary of the creeds and judged every article of them at the bar of what a reasonable man could accept. His opponents at Groningen and Utrecht saw the direction, and the dictionary says they saw it rightly.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the order set by the prophet: “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) is the standard to which every method is brought, philosophy included. Reason is a good servant and the Reformed have never despised it; Scripture is the judge, and reason is not the judge of the judge. Andreae was right that Aristotle is not an article of faith, and his critics were right about where his road ran.

pos: n. (Johannes van der Waeyen, 1639–1701, professor of theology at Franeker, a Coccejan who had first been a Labadist)
etymology: Van der Waeyen, Dutch, of or from the Waai, a water-meadow or river bend; Johannes, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious.
biblical_def: Johannes van der Waeyen was minister at Leeuwarden and then at Middelburg when, in 1669, he joined himself to Jean de Labadie, left the ministry of the Reformed church, and followed that separatist community in its wanderings. Within a few years he judged the step wrong and returned, was received back, and in 1677 was made professor of theology at Franeker, where he taught for the rest of his life. He became the chief Frisian advocate of the covenant theology of Johannes Coccejus, defending it in a long and bitter exchange with the Voetian party and particularly with Herman Witsius, who was closer to him than either man would admit. He also wrote against the Socinians and against the rationalising critics of Scripture. He died at Franeker in 1701. The dictionary keeps him chiefly for the shape of his life. A man may leave the visible church out of a real hunger for holiness—that was Labadie's appeal, and it was not a frivolous one—and may discover that the separation he thought a purification was a loss, and may come back and be useful for twenty-four years. Repentance of a public error is a public mercy, and the Frisian church did well to receive him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a separatist as one that withdraws from an established church; to recant as to retract a declaration or proposition; and restoration as the act of returning to a former good state.
webster_full: SEPARATIST, n. One that withdraws from a church, or rather from an established church, to which he has belonged; a dissenter.
RECANT, v.t. [L. recanto.] To retract; to recall; to contradict a former declaration; to unsay what has been said.
RESTORATION, n. The act of replacing in a former state; renewal; re-establishment; the act of returning to a good state.
SECT, n. [L. secta.] A body or number of persons united in tenets, chiefly in philosophy or religion, but constituting a distinct party.
RECEIVE, v.t. [L. recipio.] To take, as a thing offered or sent; to admit; to take into the mind; to welcome.
scriptures: Gal 2:5
To whom we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour; that the truth of the gospel might continue with you.
But if I tarry long, that thou mayest know how thou oughtest to behave thyself in the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth.
Rom 8:28
And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose.
Therefore, brethren, stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle.
corruption_summary: Franeker Coccejan who left the Reformed ministry for the Labadist separation, judged the step wrong, returned, and taught twenty-four years.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the separatist impulse itself, in the form Labadie gave it: that because a visible church contains unconverted members, the holy must withdraw and constitute a pure communion. It is an ancient error with an attractive face, since the complaint it starts from is usually true. What it denies is the New Testament's own picture of a mixed field and a net with good and bad in it, and the plain fact that every pure community formed on this principle has needed a purer one within a generation. Van der Waeyen tried it and came back, and his coming back is worth more to the church than his covenant theology.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the honour of the visible church. “the house of God, which is the church of the living God” (1Ti 3:15) is said of a congregation with Hymenaeus and Alexander still on its roll. Holiness is pursued inside the house, under its discipline, and not by walking out of it.

pos: n. (capital of Friesland, Dutch Leeuwarden, Frisian Ljouwert; seat of the Frisian stadholders and of the provincial Reformed church)
etymology: Dutch Leeuwarden, from Old Frisian Lintwerd or Leeuwerd, a werd or dwelling-mound by the Linde water; the lion in the modern spelling is a later folk reading.
biblical_def: Leeuwarden is the chief city of Friesland, built on three dwelling-mounds above the marsh and made the seat of government by the Saxon and then the Habsburg lords of the province. Its Reformation was slow, bloody and divided. The first executions for the gospel in Friesland were carried out there in the 1530s, and among those put to death at Leeuwarden in 1531 was Sicke Freerks, beheaded for a second baptism; it was that execution, in the town where he afterwards lived, which first shook the priest Menno Simons out of his place and set him on the road to the Anabaptist leadership. The city held for Spain until 1580, when the province went over to the Republic, the Mass was forbidden, and the Reformed church was established. From that year Leeuwarden was the seat of the Frisian synod, the residence of the stadholders of the Frisian branch of the house of Nassau, and the administrative centre from which the Reformed ministry of a province full of Mennonites was organised and paid. The dictionary keeps it as the plainest Frisian instance of a hard truth: that the ground on which a Reformed church was finally planted had usually been watered first by blood shed over a doctrine that church did not hold.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a city as a large town, incorporated with certain privileges; a province as a country belonging to a kingdom or state; and a mound as an artificial elevation of earth.
webster_full: CITY, n. [L. civitas.] A large town; in a more appropriate sense, a corporate town; a town or collective body of inhabitants, incorporated and governed by particular officers.
PROVINCE, n. [L. provincia.] A country belonging to a kingdom or state, either by conquest or colonization; a region of country; a division of a kingdom.
MOUND, n. Something raised as a defense; an artificial elevation of earth; a bank; a bulwark.
MARSH, n. A tract of low land, usually or occasionally covered with water, or very wet and miry; a swamp; a fen.
MARTYR, n. [Gr. a witness.] One who suffers death in defense of the Christian faith, or in defense of any belief.

Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.

They that sow in tears shall reap in joy.
corruption_summary: Frisian capital where the first executions for the gospel were carried out in the 1530s, and which became the seat of the provincial Reformed synod after 1580.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The honest difficulty is the mixed inheritance. Leeuwarden's first martyrs died as Anabaptists, for a doctrine of baptism the later established church of the city rejected; and that established church, once it had the magistrate behind it, was not always gentle with the Mennonites who remained. The dictionary does not smooth this over. It holds believer's baptism with the 1689 Confession and therefore stands nearer those first sufferers than the Frisian synod did; and it holds that the use of the sword against a man's conscience in matters of religion was wrong when Charles the Fifth's officers did it and wrong when a Reformed magistracy did it.

The principle to recover is that the roll of the slain is kept by God and not by the party. “I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God” (Rev 6:9) does not say that every soul under that altar had every doctrine right. It says why they were killed. A town's church history is read truly only when the dead of the other party are counted in it.

pos: n. (town in northern Friesland; where Boniface was killed in 754, and a Reformed town of the Republic after 1580)
etymology: Frisian Dokkum, earlier Dockinga, from a personal name with the Frisian -inga, the people of Docko; the -um ending is the common Frisian contraction of -heim, a home.
biblical_def: Dokkum is a small walled town on the northern Frisian clay, and it is known for two things eight hundred years apart. In June 754 the Anglo-Saxon missionary Boniface, who had spent a lifetime preaching among the Germans and had come back in old age to the Frisians who had first resisted him, was killed with his companions by a heathen band near Dokkum while waiting to confirm new converts; the account is that he held up a book against the blow, and a gospel-book with a sword-cut through it was long shown as his. A church and later an abbey stood over the place. In the sixteenth century the town took the Reformation, suffered in the Frisian risings, and after 1580 was a Reformed town of the Republic with its own classis, its harbour trade, and its share in the Frisian Mennonite question. The dictionary enters it for the earlier story. Boniface was not a Reformed man and his Rome was not the dictionary's Rome; but he went where the gospel had not been preached, he went back to the hardest field when he was old, and he died with no weapon in his hand. The Reformation did not invent missionary courage. It recovered the gospel which gives such courage its only sufficient reason.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a missionary as one sent to propagate religion; heathen as pagan, gentile, unconverted to Christianity; and to preach as to pronounce a public discourse on a religious subject.
webster_full: MISSIONARY, n. One sent to propagate religion; a person sent by ecclesiastical authority to preach the gospel in a foreign or destitute country.
HEATHEN, n. [Sax. hæthen.] A pagan; a gentile; one who worships idols, or is unacquainted with the true God.
PREACH, v.i. [L. praedico.] To pronounce a public discourse on a religious subject, or from a text of Scripture; to proclaim.
APOSTLE, n. [Gr. one sent.] A person deputed to execute some important business; particularly, one of the twelve disciples sent forth to preach the gospel.
TOWN, n. Originally, an enclosure; a collection of houses enclosed by a wall or hedge; now, any collection of houses larger than a village.

corruption_summary: Frisian town where Boniface was killed by heathen in 754, and a Reformed town of the Republic from 1580.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. There is, however, a live and lazy misuse of this story in both directions. Roman writers have used Boniface to prove that the conversion of the north was papal work and the Reformation an ingratitude. Some Protestant writers have dismissed him as a papal agent, which is a sneer and not a judgment. The dictionary takes the historical record as it stands: Boniface held the doctrine of his century, including errors the Reformation afterwards named; he also carried the Scriptures to peoples who had never heard them read, and was killed for it unarmed.

The principle to recover is that the field is not chosen by the labourer's comfort. “The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few” (Mat 9:37) was Christ's own account of the shortage, and the shortage has never been of men able to go but of men willing. An old man going back to the province that had already driven him out is a rebuke to a church that measures a call by its prospects.

pos: n. (Frisian port on the Wadden Sea; the harbour of the province and a stronghold of its Mennonite and Reformed congregations)
etymology: Frisian Harns, Dutch Harlingen, from a personal name Harl or Herel with the Frisian -inga, the people of Harl.
biblical_def: Harlingen is the sea-gate of Friesland, the only deep harbour on the province's western shore, walled and fortified in the sixteenth century and from 1580 the naval and commercial port of the Frisian Republic. Its church history is the history of a port. Sailors, grain factors and refugees came and went, and with them came books; the earliest Reformation writings in Friesland arrived through such harbours, and so did the Anabaptist teachers whom Friesland received more readily than any other Dutch province. Harlingen held both communities in strength: a Reformed classis with the magistrate behind it, and large Mennonite congregations, Flemish and Frisian and Waterlander, which built their plain meeting-houses behind the street fronts and prospered in the Baltic trade. The town's Reformed ministers were therefore men who preached every week within earshot of neighbours who denied the lawfulness of their oath, their magistracy and their baptism. The dictionary keeps Harlingen for that condition, which is more like our own than most of the sixteenth century is. A church in a trading port cannot be a church of one opinion held without challenge. It must be able to say why it believes what it believes, to people who will not be impressed by the fact that the magistrate agrees.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a port as a harbour or haven; commerce as an interchange of goods or property; and a haven as a place of safety, a shelter.
webster_full: PORT, n. [L. portus.] A harbor; a haven; any bay, cove, inlet or recess of the sea or of a lake, where vessels can lie safe from injury by storms.
COMMERCE, n. [L. commercium.] An interchange or mutual change of goods, wares, productions or property of any kind, between nations or individuals.
HAVEN, n. [Sax. hæfen.] A harbor; a port; a bay or inlet of the sea where ships can ride in safety; hence, a shelter; an asylum.
MERCHANT, n. [L. mercans.] A man who trafficks or carries on trade with foreign countries, or who exports and imports goods.
GAINSAY, v.t. To contradict; to oppose in words; to deny or declare not to be true.

Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.

Jud 1:3

Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul;
corruption_summary: Frisian port where a Reformed classis and large Mennonite congregations lived side by side in the same trading streets.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live temptation in a town like this is the one the dictionary names as civility bought with silence: a tacit agreement among neighbouring congregations not to raise the questions that divide them, because trade is easier so. That is not peace and it is not love. It is the quiet retirement of doctrine from public speech, and it ends with a generation that cannot say what its own church holds or why.

The principle to recover is the minister's double duty in Titus: “to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9). A gainsayer is a man who contradicts, and the text assumes he is nearby and must be answered, not avoided. Where a Reformed church and its neighbours differ on baptism, the oath and the magistracy, charity requires that the difference be stated plainly and argued from Scripture, and both sides be left in no doubt what the other believes.

pos: n. (Frisian town, Frisian Boalsert; where Menno Simons was schooled for the priesthood, and a Reformed town after 1580)
etymology: Frisian Boalsert, Dutch Bolsward, from a personal name Bodel or Bole with Frisian werd, a dwelling-mound raised above the marsh.
biblical_def: Bolsward is one of the eleven cities of Friesland, built on a mound in the pasture country of Westergo, with a trade in cattle and butter and a great brick church of St Martin. Its place in church history is as a nursery. The Franciscan house in the town was where the young Menno Simons, born a few miles away at Witmarsum, received the training that made him a priest about 1524—a training, as he said himself afterwards, in which he had never touched the New Testament and was afraid to, lest he be led astray. The man who went on to lead the peaceable wing of the Anabaptists out of the ruin of Munster, and to give his name to the Mennonites, was formed and starved in that school. The town later took the Reformation with the province, and from 1580 had its Reformed ministry and its share of the Frisian classis, while Mennonite congregations continued in and around it. The dictionary enters Bolsward as the place where a particular corruption can be dated and named: a system of clerical training which could ordain a man to the cure of souls without putting the Scriptures into his hands, and which left him to find them later, alone, at thirty.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a priest as one who officiates in sacred offices; ignorance as want of knowledge; and a novice as one newly admitted into a religious order.
webster_full: PRIEST, n. [L. presbyter.] A man who officiates in sacred offices; among Christians, a person who officiates at the altar, or performs the rites of sacrifice.
IGNORANCE, n. [L. ignorantia.] Want of knowledge or instruction; unenlightened state of the mind; destitution of learning.
NOVICE, n. [L. novus, new.] One who is new in any business; one newly admitted to membership in a religious house or order; a probationer.
ORDAIN, v.t. [L. ordino.] To set in order; to appoint; to invest with ministerial function or sacerdotal power.
BLIND, adj. Destitute of the sense of seeing; hence, unable or unwilling to understand or judge; undiscerning.

corruption_summary: Frisian town where Menno Simons was trained for the priesthood without ever opening the New Testament, by his own later confession.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is a clerical training that withheld the Scriptures from the men it ordained. Menno's own confession is the evidence: he had been a priest for some years before he read the New Testament, and he had been taught to fear it as a book that misleads the unlearned. That was not an accident of one friary. It was the settled practice of a church which had made the priest the dispenser of a sacrament rather than a preacher of a word, and which therefore did not need him to know the word. Every error Menno afterwards had to work out painfully for himself—and some he never worked out—was the cost of that policy.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Malachi's standard for the ministry: “the priest's lips should keep knowledge” (Mal 2:7). A man who does not know the Scriptures has no business in a pulpit, however correct his ordination; and a church which ordains such men is manufacturing the false teachers it will later have to warn against. The dictionary holds that the first duty a congregation owes its minister is to see that he is taught.
